newsitem.title: USA: Head of Mexican cartel convicted on drug charges.
newsitem.headline: Head of Mexican cartel convicted on drug charges.

text.p: Drug kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego was found guilty on Wednesday of smuggling huge quantities of cocaine into the United States in a verdict the government hailed as a major victory in the war on drugs.
Garcia Abrego, 52, was convicted on all 22 counts against him, including drug-trafficking, money-laundering and bribery. He faces life in prison without parole.

The former cookie factory worker and car thief from Texas headed the Gulf cartel -- one of the world's biggest drug operations -- responsible for shipping more than 50 tons of cocaine into the United States starting in 1986, prosecutors said.
His conviction culminated a 10-year effort by law enforcement agencies in the United States and Mexico to bring him to justice, officials said.

"Today's conviction shows that no drug trafficker, no matter how big or notorious, is safe from the law. By taking (Garcia) Abrego off the streets and putting him behind bars, we are making the streets of America safer," U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno said in a statement.

U.S. drug agents here said in a press conference that Garcia Abrego's conviction was a "major step forward," but warned it would not curb the flow of illegal drugs because other traffickers would take over his territory in northern Mexico.
Garcia Abrego was ordered to forfeit $350 million in assets, well below the $1.05 billion prosecutors sought. Estimates of Garcia Abrego's total fortune range up to $15 billion.

The tall, burly Garcia Abrego appeared shaken by the verdict but only muttered to himself and looked back sternly at his family in the heavily secured courtroom of U.S. District Judge Ewing Werlein. Family members wept in the hallway moments later.
Blanca Garcia Abrego, his sister, tearfully told reporters the family was shocked. "We are very devastated," she said. "We had hoped for the best. We still hope for the best."
Defence attorney Tony Canales said he would appeal the verdict after sentencing, which Werlein set for Jan. 31.
The eight-man, four-woman jury deliberated for two days before reaching its decision in a trial that began on Sept. 16. They would not discuss their decision with reporters.

The United States made Garcia Abrego a symbol in the fight against international drug-trafficking when it placed him on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted list in March 1995 and pressured Mexico to help capture him. He was arrested in January in the northern Mexico city of Monterrey, then deported to Houston for trial.

Cartel insiders, testifying against the man they called "El Senor" (The Man) and "El Jefe" (The Boss), said Garcia Abrego began shipping marijuana in the 1970s but switched to cocaine provided by the Cali cartel in Colombia in 1986.

They said he built what became a vast empire on a foundation of death and corruption that included hits against people considered threats to the cartel and millions of dollars in bribes paid to police and public officials on both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border.

Defence attorneys said the government produced no evidence linking Garcia Abrego to the drug cartel and accused it of bringing a "show trial" to court to boost its anti-drug credentials in this election year.

Despite more than three years of continuous wiretapping of the cartel's phone conversations, prosecutors were unable to produce any recordings of Garcia Abrego or even the mention of his name on tape. But they put on more than 50 witnesses during three weeks of testimony and laid out a detailed paper trail they said demonstrated Garcia Abrego's control of the cartel.

The trial was closely watched in Mexico because of expectations it would reveal Garcia Abrego's alleged connections to top government officials. Witnesses said he paid bribes totalling $1.5 million a month to a deputy attorney general in charge of the government's anti-drug efforts, but no other officials were mentioned.

Lead prosecutor Melissa Annis refused to comment when asked if the United States had evidence that would have implicated others higher up in the Mexican goverment. She also said it was "premature" to speculate on whether a deal might be cut with Garcia Abrego to gain further information about corruption.

News reports have linked him to Raul Salinas, brother of former President Carlos Salinas. Raul Salinas is in a Mexican jail facing charges that he ordered the 1994 assassination of a ruling party official and illicitly compiled a huge personal fortune.
